To remain a Superpower, we as a nation must remain allied with our NATO allies, to stand in unison for what is morally right against the bigotry and hatred of violent, oppressive regimes — like China & Russia — in today’s  world. Consider the wisdom of Aesop …

As a youngster, I was fascinated by “Aesop’s Fables.” One story was about an old man with three sons who were always fighting.

One day, he called them together to teach them a lesson. One by one, he gave each of his sons a bundle of sticks and asked them to try to break the bundle. They each tried their best but not one of them could do so.

The old man then took the bundle of sticks, removed a few from the bundle, and gave each of his sons a stick. He asked each of his sons to break the stick, which they did with ease.

The old man then addressed his sons with these wise words,

“My sons, if you are of one mind, and unite to assist each other, you will be as this bundle of sticks, uninjured by all the attempts of your enemies; but if you are divided among yourselves, you will be broken as easily as these sticks.”

From this fable, and his recent failed, unilateral declaration of war against Iran, our president should learn what I learned as a child. We cannot “go it alone.” We should act in unison with the “bundle of nations” of which we are but one part — NATO.

comments.name: Terri McLemore

For the millions who followed Fiona-from her premature birth through her joyous life, yesterday's sad announcement was an absolute gut punch.   The fact that the whole tragedy was completely preventable adds a layer of anger and frustration to the grief and sadness.
I grew up visiting our local zoo with my Dad.  My own children loved visiting the same zoo with their Granddad.   My whole family knows my love of zoos, and I've been so lucky to visit some really special ones-San Diego, Taranga in Sydney.
I am also a parent and an educator.  I have visited zoos with my own children and their friends and taken students on zoo field trips many times over the course of my career.
My point?  There should be clear expectations set.  No running, loud voices in enclosed spaces, no tapping on glass or teasing animals, and certainly no tossing of items or food.
Many accounts of what happened here indicate that the child  was told several times to stop throwing the hat.  Why the hat was not taken by the parents after the first toss remains the open question.  I know that I would have given a reminder once, then taken the hat to hold.  Period.  No negotiation.
We are conflating the accident portion of this tragedy with the fact that it was totally preventable.
Fiona's tragic death is a sad reminder of one of the reasons educators are walking away.  No accountability or responsiblity.  Parents who can't/won't be the adults in charge.  And everyone expects empathy and grace for them.
Nope!

This piece is ostensibly about Anthropic’s IPO, but as usual, NYT readers quickly turn it into a simplistic debate about whether we should “allow” AI to be part of our lives. 

Tech bros, evil geniuses that they are, have invented this technology all by themselves, in order to make even more money. Data centers are even worse than all the other climate-destroying technology that we already rely on, and besides, “AI” gave me a wrong answer about something last week! 

When the discovery of nuclear fission led to the development of the atomic bomb, we didn’t have the choice to opt out, or to “pull the plug” as people love to say. There was no “off switch.” People knew that at the time and were tormented by it, rightfully so. 

Similarly, AI has been a serious academic topic for over half a century already, and we can’t just put the entire thing into a box, bury it in the backyard, and pretend it never happened. 

Dario Amodei has been remarkably transparent about his own ambivalence and apprehension about this technology, and for that he is largely ridiculed, not praised. The author seems to suggest that Wall Street, in all its rapacious glory, is the medicine that Anthropic needs to swallow, shareholder value being the North Star of morality. 

I’d like to suggest that we quit viewing ourselves as passive victims of AI, acknowledge its long history, and accept the fact that, just like nuclear fission, it’s now a part of the world we live in. 

Now, how do we move forward?

Prepping is stupid. So is not doing anything to be ready for a technology collapse.

The Boy Scouts moto was "Always be prepared." Millions absorbed that idea and a smaller set are following it, often excessively.

A dirty, atomic particle bomb is something that should be considered a real possibility. An enemy who wanted to deploy one could easily understand that knocking out communications systems would be a one-two blow where a third strike might not be necessary to cause maximum disruption society wide.

The main task if a dirty bomb is set off is to get out of the exposure area and to stay out as long as necessary. In some cases, that might mean for a year or longer. Your ordinary life would be disrupted, your means of earning money to buy food and shielder could be gone. You might hope you have a relative or friend in a distant location with whom you and your family could stay for six months or longer. The previously shunned, rural, areas could suddenly be in high demand.

One key to getting away from a dirty bomb would be leaving as soon as possible before massive traffic jams shutdown roads. A paper map would be vital because you would likely be forced to take winding two lanes. If you don't know how to navigate without GPS, you's be lost.

Our country has been attacking other nations around the world more or less continually for decades. Why should we assume, one, they aren't planning counterattacks and, two, they can't manage to find a way to pull one off here?

In 2006-07, I spent 9 months in New Orleans, providing post-Hurricane Katrina disaster relief. Especially towards the beginning of my stint, I drove through many neighborhoods without any FEMA trailers in the yards, any working stoplights, any city services. Coyotes running through the streets. It was the scenario many preppers are prepping FOR.

The part of this article that resonated most strongly with me was:

"'The days of being like a lone wolf, Mad Max, off on your own, a nomad — that’s kind of fantasy land,” said Cliff Colón, the Seattle-area preparedness guru who calls himself the Urban Prepper. 'I think people are moving away from that. They know that, "Hey, to survive an emergency, I have to be part of some kind of team."'"

I drove past a lot of shuttered non-denominational, standalone churches during my time in NOLA. Catholic and Mainline Protestant churches, by and large, did better, because they had national networks they could tap into immediately for relief and support (money, volunteers, food, etc.).

The first entire neighborhood that I remember being back to "normal" after weathering heavy flooding was the Vietnamese community in Michoud--because they relied on each other rather than government aid to respond and rebuild. I remember driving through their streets in August of '06 and seeing mowed grass in the yards, lights on in the windows. It was surreal; like a different planet.

There's a lesson in that: know--and care for--your neighbors.

comments.name: Tom Herndon

The cases in this article are difficult to read, the comments even more so. Parents of ASD children face a tremendous challenge, as I can personally attest. The saying goes "If you've met one child with autism, you know one child with autism." It presents  in many different ways, and those challenges may shift over time. Attempting to get a handle on things can feel like trying to grab a fistful of water. Every child is different, so by nature effective treatment will require trial, observation, and modification as needed. Every parent has to build the roadmap, there's no best-practice treatment protocol like for other conditions. 

We started ABA back in the early 2000s when there were fewer providers and less consensus on treatment protocol. Our son was essentially non-verbal at 2.5 years. I will say this, it comes down to the program manager who develops the plan (M.A. in behavior analysis), and the therapists who execute on it. This was before online training, all our therapists were field trained as they shadowed working therapists.   Our son had two 3-hour sessions a day, four days a week, plus an hour a week with a speech pathologist and an occupational therapist. Most weeks, it was about 30  hours from 2.5 years til 1st grade. Properly done, ABA can work wonders, but the plan and the practitioners must be fully committed to success. Finding them is likely much harder now. There is an important racial dimension to how our presidential archetype collapsed. Since World War II, Americans came to expect a specific patrician model: tall, fit, conservatively dressed, well-educated, & above all restrained—a dignified white male suited to embody the office. George H.W. Bush was a restoration of that ideal after Ronald Reagan, who—though the first of our modern outsiders—still looked & sounded the part, even if he was less patrician.
Restraint, however, carries populist costs. Refusing to march to Baghdad hurt the elder Bush politically, though it was the right call. His son moved the office toward folksy anti-intellectualism—going all the way to Baghdad with disastrous results—followed by years of polite denial because "you can't say that about a U.S. president." Even Obama, breaking the racial barrier, adhered strictly to the old code of cool, unflappable restraint.
Then came Trump. Ironically, he broke the mold by adopting the exact loud, theatrical, grievance-driven persona that, when attached to Black public figures, has long been dismissed as the "angry Black man" stereotype. In better suits, backed by inherited wealth, he shattered what remained of the George Washington myth—a myth that, despite the glaring moral hypocrisies of the Founding era, nonetheless served a useful purpose by establishing behavioral guardrails.
Those guardrails are gone, leaving us with nothing but a loud, self-dealing, sleazy salesman-caudillo. Where do we go from here?

Ukraine would need to tolerate the loss of territory (although not accept the loss in legal terms) and agree not to begin an insurgency. But stopping future conflicts will likely require the presence of international peacekeepers for several generations, which Russia will not accept.

I find it hard to see any prospects for a negotiated solution.

Harsh looks like getting grilled at the 52nd Precinct.  For an instant evaluation - just look at your shadow. Direct light for work/tasking vs. ambient for everything else.  

Fluorescent bridged the gap nicely, but the blueish color-temp
wasn't ideal.  Fine for sweat shops & fast-food outlets, but not so much for attorneys' offices or most sit-down joints. At home; great for basements & garages, full stop.  Living spaces got a warmish-update in the 90s with HALOGEN and their lovely dimmers!  We could now really dial-in a personalized atmosphere/vibe. 

My small 20s Craftsman (light-cream, dark wood) positively glows from a single Torchiere-floor lamp - its soft-luminosity all around me. (For reading I can crank it up, or use a nearby goose-neck lamp.)  I have a strong preference for indirect-lighting; the warm ambiance that a nice bounce gives light. Another method is DIFFUSION; anything from a hunk of translucent fabric to glass-brick or color-gels.  I just like to bask in a lamp's GLOW - not its GLARE!

Photographers also know what the wrong WHITE BALANCE can do to a pic. The latest LEDs are both dim-able and have a range of color-temps!  So cool, right!

AVAILABLE LIGHT and wall color will mitigate...

I was always an outsider, trying to make sense of a national identity in flux. Since moving away in the late 90s, I have often observed that Russia has seemed to succumb to the apathetic, incipiently and interpersonally violent culture described here, but that was not at all a foregone conclusion when progressive politicians like Yevlentsky were speaking out. Very thoughtful essay.

Each of these films, as the sci-fi genre did years ago, use allegory and metaphor to describe the indescribable, and what it is to have so much of life numbed and unspoken, 

Most of us have no idea what it is to live under such soul numbing duress for generations.

Both Russia and China suffer from differing, but equally harsh, levels of communist-authoritarianism in which the state stands in for all.   Given the death tolls in both countries since 1917, depending on one's sources, range from 60-148M, these are apocalyptic totals, exceeding Nazi Germany's.

To put those numbers in perspective, the very rough estimates for all deaths due to religious wars, AD, are about 27M.  15M coming from Islam (usually against non-believers), and 12M from Christianity (also against non believers, often one form of the religion against the other.)  See the insane 100 Year War.

All of which points to the duality of human nature, and the importance of character.  We hand power over to those of great ambition and often questionable character.  Of course they usually get worse the longer they stay. Would that humanity govern with far more limited forms of executive power, such as requiring national referendums to address administrative abuses.

These bleak films remind us we collectively still have a long way to go, but they give voice to the voiceless.  For now that is one less degree of repression, hopefully reversing the tide back towards free speech for millions.

The most hysterical anti AI voices are drowning out any discussion of the actual benefits. So here is just one example of many of the benefits.

A path to quicker, cheaper, more accurate Alzheimer’s tests —

A Massachusetts General Brigham / MGH Institute of Health Professions study validating spontaneous speech acoustics against the blood biomarker plasma p-tau217 and APOE-ε4 genetic status (Dadgostar et al., 2026), alongside broader clinical validation of p-tau217 blood testing in preclinical Alzheimer's.

Researchers recorded short, natural speech samples from cognitively unimpaired older adults and trained machine-learning models to detect subtle acoustic shifts in voice quality and spectral stability. When cross-referenced against plasma p-tau217 blood levels, the speech-based AI models classified preclinical biological Alzheimer's risk with up to 77% accuracy—outperforming standard cognitive tests (47%) before any outward memory symptoms appeared (Dadgostar et al., 2026).

Perhaps our susceptibility to distraction is not a modern failing but an ancient survival mechanism. A hunter concentrating on stalking game still needed to allow his attention to be diverted by a rustle in the grass behind him. The ability to interrupt our concentration could mean the difference between life and death.

What has changed is the environment competing for that attention. When every Facebook post announces "BREAKING NEWS," nothing is breaking news. Repeated exposure dulls our response, so that when something genuinely consequential occurs, it fails to stand out.

This brings us back to Bernstein's observation about satire and reality. Imagine Eisenhower making some of the statements that now pass almost unnoticed when Trump makes them. What might once have dominated headlines can become routine through repetition.

Perhaps the danger is not that we've lost our capacity for sustained attention, but that repeated exposure, compounded by the way journalists frame extraordinary statements, can gradually change our standards for recognizing what deserves alarm. When the absurd becomes familiar, we risk mistaking normalization for normality.

Thar seems straightforward, not surprising. I wish the author had gone into more biological detail about what strains of microbes are included - that was unhelpfully glossed over.

And I didn't appreciate the bait-and-switch of the "AI" headline. We are already swamped with AI news on a daily basis, so considering that this shelf-stable sourdough starter doesn't involve AI whatsoever, can we please just stick to the facts?

The root of this crisis lies at the intersection of unregulated lithium-ion battery overloading and aging electrical infrastructure that was never designed to handle modern power demands. Walking through my neighborhood of Bedford-Stuyvesant, it is impossible to ignore the sheer volume of e-bikes and mopeds—and the hazardous charging setups inside residential buildings whose wiring is visibly outdated and not up to code.

​Addressing this requires immediate, coordinated action across both the public and private sectors:

​Municipal Infrastructure: The City must prioritize the rapid rollout of safe, accessible, outdoor public charging and battery-swapping stations, particularly in high-density neighborhoods like Bed-Stuy where delivery workers and commuters rely heavily on micromobility.

​Private Sector Accountability: Landlords and property management companies cannot continue to pass the risk onto tenants. They must invest directly in dedicated, fire-rated, code-compliant charging rooms equipped with proper ventilation and suppression systems.
​

​We should not have to wait for another preventable tragedy to enforce basic safety standards. Protecting our communities requires treating electrical capacity and safe battery infrastructure as urgent public safety priorities today.

Thanks for your appreciation piece of Marian Anderson, one of many steps toward equal rights (and, alas, with recent backlash, many steps to go).

Completely agree about "The Verge." When I first read the script it blew me away. Here was a writer back in 1921 using terms like the "Other," a concept/term that only became prevalent in academia in the last few decades. And here was a "madwoman in the 'attic,'" long before Gilbert and Gubar wrote their groundbreaking feminist literary study. What must have 1920 audiences and drama critics thought of so radical a play? Even today some of the protagonist Claire's speeches are eyebrow raising.

When I taught it to graduate students, many of them in the class decided to write their seminar paper on it.

Even with some cuts (I'm deducing since the script is in 4 acts), the play is a little too talky onstage, but the actors were game for keeping the pace going. And the scene design and blocking were  outstanding.

comments.name: just ben
comments.body:
Praise for writing about Marian Anderson. Besides being an extraordinary singer who brought listeners to tears, she projected great dignity--no matter what she felt inside. 

But are you overlooking the obvious? You mention that she sometimes sang with eyes closed. That is also the best way to listen to music (unless, of course, it's opera.) 

If you listen to Marian Anderson recordings--granted that the sound quality is not up to current standards--you can't fail to be deeply moved. (You need not even know who's singing.) Without taking anything away from her--nobody should ever do that!--she achieved success despite racism because there was no gainsaying her singing.

Music is what happens with your eyes closed. Rock and roll "musicians" have no talent, and the ruckus they emit busts your ears. That's why they resort to weird costumes, hairdos, strutting, ear-splitting amplification, flashing lights, disco balls, and so forth.  

But now, even good musicians, playing timeless masterpieces, have sunk to mugging for the camera in, for example, Facebook and youtube videos. 

In our video-driven age, we fall into the trap of paying more attention to images (and image) than sound and text. Recalling Marian Anderson reminds us of the price we're paying.

comments.name: bill steigerwald
comments.body: Obits were often considered the purgatory or the gulag of the  newspaper biz. It's where interns and washed up hacks were stationed. It was not a place for good writing.  At the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, the deaths of the un-famous were often reduced to having their names, ages and places of death plugged into brisk templates that had spaces to fill in the funeral parlor and places of interment . At the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette in the 1990s the editor, John Craig, was smart enough to realize the power of the obit. He instituted a policy that all writers and reporters, even the hotshots, had to spend a week doing local obituaries that were well written and of appropriate length  -- nice little feature stories on deadline, as it were.  It was a genius move -- not only did it give value to readers and honor to the departed, it was a smart PR move. Obits of local grocers, doctors  and political hacks  were read by their loved ones and sometimes hundreds of their friends. Writing an obit took a few hours -- calls to the funeral home and a call or two to get quotes and anecdotes from a relative or friend of the dead. Once I got a call from the wife of my obit subject.  She said it had made her cry and she liked it so much she put it in her husband's casket.

comments.name: Critique
comments.body: Wokeness sometimes becomes an exercise in virtue signaling. Inclusivity and diversity are worthwhile goals in their own right, and I believe most people genuinely support these principles. However, they may not necessarily be everyone's top priority, and why should they have to be? People have different concerns, values, and priorities, and that doesn't mean they are indifferent to these causes. The problem arises when such causes are hijacked by those more interested in demonstrating their own moral superiority than advancing the cause itself. It becomes obnoxious when the conversation shifts from “these values matter” to “you don't care enough” or “I care more than you do.” In my view, that is precisely where Wokeness 1.0 lost its way—when genuine advocacy gave way to moral posturing and competitive virtue signaling.

The DSA needs to abandon identity politics?

Democratic politicians  hid behind the convenient veneer of identity politics for decades while embracing neoliberalism. Democrats abandoned their  FDR roots in their drive to keep  their donors happy. 

Sure, the  DSA may need to de-emphasize identity politics and wokeness, but  why the emphasis on this now,   when  housing, groceries, college and health care are soaring out of reach for too many Americans?

Who is going to pressuring Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer to abandon their version of identity politics?  The ones where we hear about "historic firsts,"  while more meaningful historic firsts  - like the passage of  universal health care,  paid family leave and a minimum wage increase pegged to inflation - disappear into the circular file.

If the Democrats begin meaningful work on these issues,  there won't be much oxygen left in the room for "wokeness"  and "identity.'

This needs to be a worker led movement built by and for the working people of this nation that helps people build a better life for them and their family today.

Proto-Indo-European Root. The word traces back to the PIE root *pós or *pósti, meaning "after" or "behind". 

Because postumus frequently referred to children born after a father's death, Late Latin writers mistakenly linked the ending -umus to humus ("dirt" or "earth") and humare ("to bury"). They inserted an h to create posthumus, shifting the literal sense from simply "last" to "after burial".

comments.name: A geologist

Thank you for reminding we can't allow the super El Niño to suck all the air out of the room, importantly, other weather and thermodynamic factors still very much exist.

For one, researchers are puzzled and alarmed by the earliest major sudden stratospheric warming on record, it has suppressed the anticipated formation of the stratospheric Polar Vortex (SPV). For those not familiar, the SPV is much higher than the better known tropospheric Jet Stream.

The SPV is a wave of circulating very cold air that forms in winter and dissipates in spring. The Jet Stream and SPV are seperate but can interfere with each other, such as when warming and heat domes reaches high in the atmosphere, causing them to wobble and break up—what we see now.

Widespread unprecedented summer warmth has continued into fall. Researchers don't know what the impact will be, but are increasingly saying its becoming more likely the Super El Niño will continue to warm and impact the normal development of the SPV.

As the article notes, the confluence of cascading complexities of the earth's thermodynamic phenomena create greater impacts on the ground. These complexities are more and more important because the earth's systems are complex and dynamic, one impacts the other to create climate and weather: oceans, land, air—all their complex processes.

Let's end, we really, really, do not want a continually warming stratosphere, it is anticipated to continue to warm in pulses or phases, but... Period.

A book came out some years ago.  About the great cat massacre in Paris around the year 1700. Give or take.

The author touched on a lot of things.  And one of them was hunger.  Not only hunger but famine.  There was no safety net back then.  If you didn't eat--

--'cause you had no money to buy food--

--then you starved.  The End.  

Carlo Collodi's Italy (in the mid 1800's) a bit like that.   The untutored poor, the powerless, the helpless-

--they went to the wall.  After a lifetime spent toiling for a pittance, they died.  The way Candlewick died.  Alone and miserable.  

"We're not in Kansas anymore, Toto."  

Nor in America during the '30's.  Despite all that poverty and unemployment.  

Let alone America nowadays. Where (for all our gripes and dissatisfaction) we're doing pretty well.  

I laughed and laughed--

--reading about Pinocchio doing guard duty over a farmer's chickens.  And those polecats!  They'd come to an arrangement with the dog.  So he looked the other way when they came sneaking in. 

But they're caught by that farmer.  Who proposes to turn them over to the local inn keeper.  Who'll prepare a delectable sweet 'n' sour sauce--

--and advertise the creatures as rabbit!   

Corruption!  It's endemic.  It's a dog eat dog world we live in.  You get by as you can--

--especially if you're poor.  And live in a poor country--

--like Italy in the mid 1800's.  

It all comes out in that dour tale of Pinocchio.  

Thanks, NYT.

I had no idea. 

So many illustrators!  And those fanciful, elaborate drawings  lavished on a poor puppet--

--longing to be a boy.  

But what have they done with the original book?  

Years ago, I bought that book.  Illustrations?  I don't remember any.  It was all pure prose--

--and boy!  What bald, bleak prose it was!  And the dour, saturnine picture it gives us of human life. 

For instance--

--the scene where our puppet is locked up, doing sentry duty over a farmer's chickens.  And the polecats come roaming in.  

The dog, they ask.  What happened to the dog?  

The dog?  He's dead

Oh, they exclaim.  Poor dog.  He was so sympathetic.  

Sympathetic?  Of course!  He was corrupt.  He let the creatures carry off some chickens--

--provided they left him one.  Share and share alike.   

And his grieving master never suspected a thing.  

But Pinocchio sounds the alarm.  The polecats are apprehended.  And told (with great relish) what the farmer has in store for them.  

They'll be killed.  Of course.  And then--

--he'll sell them to the local inn keeper.  Who'll put them on the menu.  Advertising them not as polecats--

--but rabbit! 

Years back, I was reading this to my son.  And laughing so hard, I could hardly get the words out.  

Farmers, dogs, and polecats!  All corrupt!  All doing deals on the sly.  It's a wicked world out there.  

And the moral of the story is--

--you'd better keep your wits about you.  

You'll need 'em.  

Thanks, NYT.

There are quite a few phrases that only my family use- too many to list here, if I’m honest, and many of them I don’t pick up on, as I’m so used to hearing them.

The most obvious ones are the Yiddish and Hebrew integrations. I come from a Jewish family, and while neither language is fluently spoken within my house, it seeps through the cracks as slang. The two words/phrases most commonly used are ‘Meshuga’ (Yiddish, meaning crazy) and ‘Ein ba aya’ (Hebrew, no problem), as both are frequently necessary within my house!

Beyond that, in my house, ceiling lights are called owls (Yes, like the animal). This comes from an instance during a holiday lights tour at the Morton Arboretum, where my mother mistook a partially obscured chandelier-like display for an owl. "But Calyx," you say, "Those things look nothing alike!" I know, dear reader. I don’t know how she managed it either.
